mainTopic: Attaching to another's vow (התפסה): does one attach to the original state or the later state? This is applied to a woman 'in your footsteps' and to a husband's 'and I' and 'I am a נזיר, and you'.
overview: Before this section, the גמרא asked about a woman who attached herself to another woman's נזירות, after which the first woman's husband annulled the first vow. מר זוטרא says this is the same as רמי בר חמא's question: when someone vows 'like the flesh of a שלמים', does he mean the meat's early forbidden state or its later permitted state? The גמרא first says the cases are different, and then brings another version that says they are certainly the same. Next it asks what happens if the second woman said 'I am a נזירה in your footsteps'. It tries to answer from the משנה's case of a husband who says 'and I' to his wife's vow and cannot annul it. The proof is rejected, because 'and I' counts as upholding her vow, so the husband case proves nothing. Finally the גמרא sets the משנה's case 'I am a נזיר, and you' against a ברייתא that seems to rule differently. רב יהודה changes the ברייתא's wording to match the משנה, while אביי keeps it and says the ברייתא is a case where the husband made his vow depend on hers.

steps.title: מר זוטרא links the question to רמי בר חמא's question
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא בריה דרב מרי says the question about the two women is really the same as רמי בר חמא's question about someone who says 'This is upon me like the flesh of a שלמים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא, son of רב מרי, said: This question is the same as רמי בר חמא's question. רמי בר חמא asked: If someone says, 'This is upon me like the flesh of a שלמים,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא says the question we just asked is not a new one, because it is the same as a question רמי בר חמא already asked. He quotes רמי בר חמא's question to set up the comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat of a שלמים is forbidden before its blood is sprinkled and permitted to eat afterward. So when someone compares an object to it, we do not know which stage he means. מר זוטרא sees the same doubt in the case of the woman whose vow was later annulled.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the same as
Asked (raised a question with no clear answer)
This is upon me, a phrase that makes something forbidden by a vow
A peace-offering, whose meat may be eaten after the blood is sprinkled
What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Mari, said:
This is the same as [the question] of Rami bar Chama.
phrases.notes: "This" means the question just asked, about the second woman who attached herself to a vow that was later annulled.

phrases.english: For Rami bar Chama asked:
"This is upon me like the flesh of a peace-offering": what is the law?
phrases.notes: He is saying this about some ordinary object, trying to forbid it to himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי אָמַר: הַאי, הַיְינוּ דְּרָמִי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the question asked just before this section to an existing question of רמי בר חמא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The question about the second woman is the same as רמי בר חמא's question about vowing 'like the flesh of a שלמים'.

steps.title: The two sides of רמי בר חמא's question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the doubt. When a person attaches a vow to something, does he attach it to its original forbidden state or to its later permitted state?
steps.simpleTranslation: When a person attaches his vow to something, does he attach it to its original state? Or perhaps he attaches it to its later, permitted state?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly what רמי בר חמא was unsure about. This sets up why מר זוטרא thinks it matches the women's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he means the original state, the meat was forbidden then, so his vow works. If he means the later state, the meat becomes permitted after the blood is sprinkled, so his vow does nothing. The women's case seems the same: does the second woman mean the first vow before the annulment or after it?

keyTerms.meaning: Attaches a vow to something else (התפסה)
In its original state
Or perhaps
In its 'cooled-down' state, meaning its later permitted state

phrases.english: When a person attaches [his vow to something],
does he attach it to its original state,
or perhaps he attaches it to its later, permitted state?
phrases.notes: Literally 'in its coolness': the stage after the holiness has 'cooled off' and the meat may be eaten.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מַתְפֵּיס אִינִישׁ, בְּעִיקָּרָא מַתְפֵּיס, אוֹ דִּלְמָא בִּצְנָנָא מַתְפֵּיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the doubt behind the question quoted in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a person who attaches a vow mean the item's original forbidden state or its later permitted state?

steps.title: The cases are not really comparable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects מר זוטרא's comparison. Even after sprinkling, שלמים meat stays somewhat holy. But an annulled vow is completely gone, so attaching to its 'later state' would mean attaching to nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they comparable? There, since he said 'This is upon me like the flesh of a peace-offering', even though after its blood is sprinkled he may eat it outside, it is still holy. But here, if you think she attaches to the later, permitted state, her husband already annulled the vow!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on מר זוטרא and says the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With שלמים, even the later stage still has holiness, so a vow attached to it has something real to grab onto. With the annulled נזירות, the later stage is nothing at all, because the husband wiped it out. So no one would attach to that later state, and the women's case does not depend on רמי בר חמא's doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they comparable? (a way of rejecting a comparison)
Its blood was sprinkled on the altar
Outside the Temple courtyard
It is still holy
Annulled (a husband canceling his wife's vow)
If it enters your mind, if you would think

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is saying שלמים meat becomes totally ordinary after sprinkling. It may be eaten, even outside the courtyard, but it is still holy. That leftover holiness is the whole difference.

phrases.english: Are they comparable?
There, since he said
"This is upon me like the flesh of a peace-offering,"

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דִּלְאַחַר שֶׁנִּזְרַק דָּמוֹ
phrases.english: even though after its blood is sprinkled
he may eat it outside [the courtyard],
it is still holy.
But here,

phrases.aramaic: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בִּצְנָנָא קָא מַתְפֵּיס
phrases.english: if you think she attaches to the later, permitted state,
phrases.notes: "She" is the second woman, who attached herself to the first woman's vow.

phrases.english: her husband annulled it for her!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison made in steps 1-2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between the women's case and רמי בר חמא's question, not רמי בר חמא's question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: After sprinkling, שלמים still has holiness, but an annulled vow is completely empty, so the 'later state' option does not really exist in the women's case.

steps.title: Another version: it is certainly the same question
steps.stepSummary: Some say the comparison holds after all. The women's question is definitely the same as רמי בר חמא's question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: It is certainly the same as רמי בר חמא's question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version that does not accept the rejection in step 3. It says the two questions really are the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this version, the difference raised in step 3 does not break the comparison. The core doubt is the same in both cases: does a person mean the earlier state or the later one? So the women's question stands or falls with רמי בר חמא's question.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (another version)
Certainly

steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions. One says the women's case is different from רמי בר חמא's question, because an annulled vow leaves nothing to attach to. The other says it is certainly the same question.

phrases.english: Some say:
It is certainly the same as [the question of] Rami bar Chama.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, הַיְינוּ דְּרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא וַדַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version that does not accept step 3's rejection and confirms step 1's comparison.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The difference about leftover holiness does not change the basic shared doubt of earlier state versus later state.

steps.title: New question: 'I am a nazirite in your footsteps'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks a new question. What if the second woman said to the first, 'I am a נזירה in your footsteps,' and then the first woman's vow was annulled?
steps.simpleTranslation: If she said to her, 'I am a nazirite in your footsteps,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a different wording the second woman might use. The next step will explain the two sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the second woman simply joined the first woman's vow. Now she uses the words 'in your footsteps', which might mean she will follow the first woman in everything, including the annulment.

keyTerms.meaning: I am hereby a נזירה
In your footsteps, following you

phrases.english: If she said to her,
phrases.notes: The second woman is speaking to the first woman, who made the נזירות vow.

phrases.english: "I am a nazirite in your footsteps": what is the law?
phrases.notes: The case is that the first woman's husband later annulled her vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about a different wording, after finishing the discussion of רמי בר חמא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the second woman's status if she said 'in your footsteps' and the first woman's vow was annulled?

steps.title: The two sides of the 'footsteps' question
steps.stepSummary: Does 'in your footsteps' mean she follows the first woman in everything, so she is free once the first is annulled? Or does it mean like the first woman was before the annulment, so she stays bound?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does 'I am in your footsteps' mean in every matter, so she is permitted? Or perhaps it means like the first woman was before her husband annulled her vow, so she is forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the two possible meanings of 'in your footsteps'. The next steps try to answer this from the משנה about a husband who says 'and I'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'footsteps' means following her completely, then when the first woman's vow is annulled, the second woman is free too. If it means copying the first woman's vow as it was when she spoke, before the annulment, then the second woman stays a נזירה. It is the same 'earlier state or later state' doubt, now tied to these specific words.

keyTerms.meaning: In every matter
She is permitted
Before
She is forbidden (bound by the vow)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the exact words a person uses when attaching to someone else's vow can decide whether she follows that vow's later fate or only its starting point.

phrases.english: "I am in your footsteps"
means in every matter, and so she is permitted.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כְּמִיקַּמֵּי דְּלֵיפַר לַהּ בַּעְלַהּ,
phrases.english: Or perhaps [it means] like before her husband annulled it for her,
and so she is forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two sides of the question asked in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'in your footsteps' mean following the first woman in everything, including the annulment, or only her vow as it was before the annulment?

steps.title: A proof from the husband who says 'and I'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the משנה: a husband who joins his wife's נזירות by saying 'and I' cannot annul her vow. If attaching meant attaching only to the original vow, he should be able to annul hers and keep his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A woman vowed to be a נזירה. Her husband heard and said 'And I.' He cannot annul her vow. Now, if attaching yourself to someone's vow means attaching to how it was at the start, he should be able to annul her vow and keep his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the 'in your footsteps' question from step 6 using a משנה. This step builds the first half of the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that the husband cannot annul. If his vow were attached only to her vow's original state, annulling hers would not touch his, so nothing should stop him. The fact that he cannot annul suggests his vow is tied to hers all the way through.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source as a proof
'And I': the husband joins his wife's vow
To annul: a husband's power to cancel his wife's vow
In its original state, as it was at the start

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A woman who vowed to be a nazirite,
and her husband heard and said 'And I' —
he cannot annul her vow.
phrases.notes: For now the גמרא assumes this is because annulling hers would cancel his too. Step 9 gives a different reason.

phrases.english: And if it should enter your mind
that when one says to her 'I am in your footsteps' —
he attaches himself to the original state of the vow,
then let him annul her vow
and keep his own standing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the doubt raised in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That attaching to a vow means attaching to the vow throughout, not just its original state
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: a husband who said 'and I' cannot annul his wife's vow

steps.title: Conclusion of the proof: the second woman is free too
steps.stepSummary: So he must attach to the whole matter, and that is why he cannot annul. Then a woman who said 'in your footsteps' is also freed when the first woman's vow is annulled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from this that he attaches himself to the whole thing. That is why he cannot annul. So a woman who said 'I am in your footsteps' is also free once the first vow is annulled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof and applies it to the question from step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If attaching means following the vow in everything, then whatever happens to the first vow happens to the second. So the second woman goes free when the first woman's vow is annulled. This would settle step 6's question in favor of its first side, 'in every matter, so she is permitted.'

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: we can conclude
In the whole matter, in every stage of the vow
Permitted, released from the vow

phrases.english: Rather, is it not so? Learn from it
that he attaches himself to the whole matter,
and that is why he cannot annul.
So a woman who said 'I am in your footsteps,'
she too is permitted!
phrases.notes: She is freed once the first woman's husband annuls the first woman's vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof set up in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: The second woman is freed when the first woman's vow is annulled
steps.raayaSupportSource: The husband who says 'and I' cannot annul

steps.title: Rejection: 'And I' counts as upholding her vow
steps.stepSummary: No proof. He may attach only to the original state. The real reason he cannot annul is that saying 'and I' is like saying 'your vow is upheld.' If he asks a חכם to release him from that upholding, he can annul.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really he attaches to the original vow. But here, when he said 'and I,' it is as if he told her 'Your vow is upheld.' If he asks to be released from his upholding, he can annul. If not, he cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof by giving a different reason why the husband cannot annul.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's problem is not that his vow is tied to hers. By joining her vow, he showed he approves of it, and that counts as הקמה (upholding). Once a vow is upheld, a husband cannot annul it unless he first gets released from his upholding through a שאלה to a חכם. So the 'in your footsteps' question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really: the גמרא keeps the first approach
'It is upheld for you': the husband confirms his wife's vow
Asks a חכם to release him (שאלה)
Upholding: the husband confirming his wife's vow

steps.confusionAlert: The husband is not blocked because his vow is linked to hers. He is blocked because joining her vow counts as approving it.

phrases.english: No, really he attaches himself to the original state,
and here, since he said to her 'And I' —
it is as if he said 'It is upheld for you.'
And if he asks to be released from his upholding —
he can annul,
and if not — he cannot.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the husband case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The husband cannot annul because 'and I' counts as הקמה, not because his vow is tied to hers in everything.
steps.whatToRemember: The husband who says 'and I' cannot annul because he has upheld her vow. So the 'in your footsteps' question is still unanswered.

steps.title: The משנה: 'I am a נזיר, and you'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a husband said 'I am a נזיר, and you,' and she answered 'Amen.' He can annul hers, and his own vow still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I am a נזיר, and you,' and she said 'Amen.' He can annul her vow, and his own vow stays.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting another case from the משנה. This sets up the contradiction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the husband vowed first and she joined him. Since her vow is her own, he can annul it, and his vow is not affected.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I am a נזיר, and you': the husband invites his wife to join
Amen: her way of accepting the vow

phrases.english: 'I am a nazirite, and you,'
and she said 'Amen' —
he annuls hers,
and his stands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He can annul her vow, and his own vow stays in force.

steps.title: A ברייתא that seems to contradict the משנה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that in the same case both are bound, and if she does not say 'Amen,' both are free, because he made his vow depend on hers. This seems to clash with the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised a contradiction: 'I am a נזיר, and you,' and she said 'Amen.' Both are forbidden. If she did not, both are permitted, because he hung his vow on her vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets a ברייתא against the משנה it just quoted. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says his vow depends on hers, so the two vows are tied together. The משנה says he can annul hers and keep his own, which treats them as separate. That is the contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contradicted: a source that clashes is brought
Forbidden, bound by the vow
He hung his vow on hers, made it depend on hers

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
'I am a nazirite, and you,' and she said 'Amen' —
both are forbidden,
and if not —
phrases.notes: Meaning, if she did not answer 'Amen.'

phrases.english: both are permitted,
because he made his vow depend on her vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה quoted in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that he annuls hers and his stands
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא ties his vow to hers. That seems to clash with the משנה's ruling that he can annul hers while his own stays.

steps.title: רב יהודה changes the wording of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers the contradiction by changing the wording of the ברייתא so that it says what the משנה says.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Learn the ברייתא this way: 'He can annul her vow, and his own vow stays in place.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the clash from step 11. He says the ברייתא should be learned with different words, so it agrees with the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא as we have it said 'both are bound.' רב יהודה replaces that with the משנה's ruling: the husband may annul her vow, and his own נזירות still holds. Once the wording matches, the two sources no longer disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn it as / teach it this way. The גמרא uses this word when it fixes how a source should read.
He annuls. A husband's power to cancel his wife's vow.
Stands, stays in force.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: Teach it this way:
phrases.notes: Learn the ברייתא from step 11 with these words in place of 'both are bound.'

phrases.english: "He annuls hers, and his stands."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11 by changing the ברייתא's wording so it matches the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the source so it matches the other source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא really rules that both are bound, which goes against the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא should say 'he annuls hers and his stands,' exactly like the משנה.

steps.title: אביי keeps the ברייתא and says it is a different case
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the ברייתא does not need to be changed. It describes a husband who made his own vow depend on his wife's vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: You can even keep the ברייתא the way it is written. The ברייתא is talking about a case where he said to her 'I am a נזיר and you,' so he hung his vow on her vow.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a second answer to the clash. He keeps the ברייתא's words and explains that it is talking about a different case from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, the husband in the ברייתא tied his own נזירות to his wife's. That is why both are bound if she says 'Amen,' and both are free if she does not. In the משנה his vow did not depend on hers, so he can annul hers and his own still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: As it teaches, keeping the text exactly as written.
A teaching of the תנאים that was left out of the משנה.
Hangs, makes it depend on.
His vow on her vow.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to settle the משנה and the ברייתא. רב יהודה changes the ברייתא's wording. אביי keeps it and says that in the ברייתא the husband made his vow depend on hers, so his vow stands or falls with hers.
steps.confusionAlert: The words 'הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר וְאַתְּ' look almost the same in both sources. אביי's point is not about new words. It is that in the ברייתא's case the husband means his vow to depend on hers.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the same words can create a separate vow or a vow that depends on someone else's, and the result changes completely.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
You can even say it is as it teaches,
The baraita is a case where he said to her:
"I am hereby a nazir, and you,"
for he is hanging his vow on her vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the same קשיא. It keeps the ברייתא as written, where step 12 changed its wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the two sources describe different situations
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא describe the same case and rule differently, unless we change the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the ברייתא the husband made his vow depend on hers, so both vows stand or fall together. In the משנה his vow does not depend on hers, so he can annul hers and keep his own.
